title: Where to Eat Kalguksu & Sujebi (Korean Noodle Soups) in Seoul: 4 Bib Gourmand Picks for Cold Days
html:
When the weather turns cold in Seoul, a lot of locals head straight for a bowl of kalguksu ("knife noodles" — wide, chewy wheat noodles cut by hand and cooked in a hot broth) or sujebi (soft, hand-torn dough pieces in the same kind of broth). Both are simple, filling, usually not spicy, and cheap by restaurant standards — most bowls run around ₩10,000–16,000 (about $7–12 USD). If you've never tried either, think of them as Korea's answer to a bowl of hearty noodle soup on a cold day back home.

Here are four small, long-running noodle soup spots that have all earned a MICHELIN Guide Seoul Bib Gourmand — an award for great food at a reasonable price, not fine dining. A nice bonus for first-time visitors: all four are walk-in restaurants that manage their own tables, so you don't need to figure out a Korean reservation app before you go.

1. Hwangsaengga Kalguksu — Bukchon, Jongno-gu

This small restaurant sits right in Bukchon Hanok Village, Seoul's famous neighborhood of traditional wooden houses, so it's an easy lunch stop if you're already walking around there. It's known for handmade noodles in a light, savory broth — the kind of simple bowl that's been drawing a loyal local crowd for years, which is part of why it keeps showing up on the Bib Gourmand list.

A beginner tip: the menu is short and mostly just variations of kalguksu, so you can't really go wrong by pointing at any photo on the menu or wall. Portions are generous, so one bowl is usually plenty for one person.

  • Address: 78 Bukchon-ro 5-gil, Jongno-gu, Seoul
  • Hours: Reported as open daily from roughly 11:00–21:30, with no confirmed regular closing day — but hours can change, so check a map app (Naver Map or Kakao Map) before you go.
  • Good to combine with: A morning walking through Bukchon Hanok Village's alleys, or a visit to nearby Gyeongbokgung Palace.

2. Limbyungjoo Sandong Kalguksu — Seocho-gu

This spot's specialty is a clam-broth kalguksu — the noodles are cooked in a broth made from clams instead of the more common anchovy or chicken stock, which gives the soup a slightly briny, seafood-forward flavor. It also serves Pyeongyang-style jumbo dumplings (wangmandu), which are worth ordering alongside the noodles if you're hungry.

Something worth knowing before you plan your trip: this restaurant is closed on Mondays. On other days it's generally open from 11:00, closing around 21:30 on weekdays and 21:00 on weekends.

  • Address: 65 Gangnam-daero 37-gil, Seocho-gu, Seoul
  • Closed: Mondays
  • Good to combine with: Shopping or sightseeing around the greater Gangnam area — check a map app for the exact walk from the nearest subway exit.

3. Samcheongdong Sujebi — Samcheong-dong, Jongno-gu

If kalguksu is "knife noodles," sujebi is its softer cousin: instead of noodles, the cook tears off small, flat pieces of dough by hand and drops them straight into the simmering broth. The texture ends up somewhere between a noodle and a dumpling — soft on the outside, a little chewy in the middle. This restaurant has been serving it in the same quiet, hanok-style building in Samcheong-dong for years.

Samcheong-dong is the street that runs alongside Gyeongbokgung Palace's eastern wall, lined with galleries and cafes, so this makes a cozy warm-up stop after walking the palace grounds on a cold day.

  • Address: 101-1 Samcheong-ro, Jongno-gu, Seoul
  • Hours: Generally open daily from around 11:00, with last orders sometime in the evening — sources don't fully agree on the exact closing time, so double-check on a map app.
  • Nearest station: Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3), Exit 1.
  • Good to combine with: Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Samcheong-dong gallery/cafe street.

4. Jeongmyeon — Near Konkuk University, Gwangjin-gu

Jeongmyeon is the smallest and most unusual spot on this list: it's a one-person operation with an open kitchen and just seven counter seats, and the menu has exactly two dishes — a white noodle soup and a red (spicy) noodle soup, both made with a broth that blends seafood, pork, and chicken. It's technically a meat-and-noodle soup rather than classic kalguksu, but it has the same warming, broth-forward comfort that fits perfectly with this list on a cold day.

⚠️ The red soup is genuinely spicy — if you're not used to Korean spice levels, it's safer to start with the white soup, which has all the same rich broth without the heat. The red version usually also comes with a small bowl of rice on the side, which helps balance the spice.

Because there are only seven seats and one chef cooking everything, lines can form at peak lunch and dinner times — going a little before or after the usual meal rush makes it easier to grab a seat.

  • Address: 88 Neungdong-ro 13-gil, Gwangjin-gu, Seoul
  • Hours: Roughly 11:30–20:00 with an afternoon break in between (sources vary slightly) — check a map app on the day you go.
  • Good to combine with: The Konkuk University (Kondae) area's student-friendly shops, cafes, and the nearby Children's Grand Park.

Quick comparison

Restaurant Neighborhood Signature Dish Good For
Hwangsaengga Kalguksu Bukchon, Jongno-gu Handmade knife-cut noodle soup A lunch break while exploring Bukchon Hanok Village
Limbyungjoo Sandong Kalguksu Seocho-gu Clam-broth kalguksu, jumbo dumplings Noodle fans who also want dumplings on the side
Samcheongdong Sujebi Samcheong-dong, Jongno-gu Hand-torn dough soup (sujebi) Warming up after visiting Gyeongbokgung Palace
Jeongmyeon Near Konkuk University White or spicy red meat-noodle soup Solo diners who don't mind a tiny 7-seat counter

💬 Got a favorite bowl of kalguksu or sujebi in Seoul, or a question about any of these spots? Drop it in the comments below — happy to help!
meta_description: 4 Michelin Bib Gourmand noodle soup spots in Seoul (kalguksu & sujebi) - walk-in, beginner-friendly comfort food for cold days.
